questions.title: TM Existence and Decidability
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
S1: For any problem if TM exist then problem may be decidable.
S2: For any problem if TM not exist then problem may be decidable.
Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: If a TM exists, the problem may be decidable (or only semidecidable). If no TM exists, the problem cannot be decidable. So only S1 is correct.

questions.title: CYK Algorithm
questions.question: Which of the following is / are true about CYK algorithm?
options: CYK is a bottom up parsing algorithm.
CYK algorithm will take O(n^3) time to verify n length string.
CYK is a dynamic programming algorithm.
CYK algorithm is used to check whether given string is a member of the language or not.
questions.solution: CYK is a bottom-up dynamic programming membership algorithm for CNF grammars running in O(n^3). All four statements are true.

questions.title: Halting Problem Not Decidable
questions.question: In which of the following machine, halting problem is not decidable?
questions.solution: Halting is decidable for FA, LBA and DPDA. It is undecidable only for Turing machines. So none of the given machines is correct.

questions.title: Decidable Problems Statements
questions.question:
Consider the following Statements:
(i) Nondisjointness problem is decidable for regular expression.
(ii) Totality problem for DPDA is decidable.
(iii) Every decidable problem is also semidecidable.
Which of the following is correct?
questions.answer: All three statements (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct.
questions.solution: (i) Intersection of regular languages is regular and emptiness is decidable. (ii) Totality (L = Sigma*) is decidable for DPDA since DPDAs are closed under complement. (iii) Decidable implies RE (semidecidable). Options were not provided in the source.

questions.title: Decidable Problem for TM
questions.question: Which of the following is decidable to turing machine?
questions.solution: The halting problem, blank tape halting problem and membership problem for recursively enumerable languages are all undecidable.

questions.title: Dead States in TM
questions.question:
Consider the following statement:
S1: In turing machine every final state is dead.
S2: In turing machine every non-final state may be dead.
Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: A TM halts on reaching a final state, so final states have no outgoing transitions (dead). A non-final state may also have no outgoing transitions (halting and rejecting). Both statements are correct.

questions.title: Incorrect Statement on RE Languages
questions.question: Which of the following is not correct?
options: If language is NOT even semidecidable, then it must be NOT RE.
If language is undecidable then it may be RE.
If a language is semidecidable but not decidable then it may be Recursive.
questions.solution: Semidecidable = RE. A semidecidable but not decidable language is by definition not recursive, so option (d) is incorrect.

questions.title: Decidable and Semidecidable Languages
questions.question: Which of the following is / are correct?
options: A language 'L' is semidecidable iff there exist a turing machine which accept L and which halts (on strings of L).
A language 'L' is decidable iff there exist a turing machine which accept 'L'.
A language is decidable iff there exist an algorithm.
questions.solution: Decidable means an algorithm (a halting TM) exists. A TM that merely accepts L makes L RE, not necessarily decidable, so (b) is false. Note: the text of option (a) was garbled in the source; it was interpreted as halting on strings of L.

questions.title: Infinite Language of DFA
questions.question: Let L = {<X> | X is a DFA and L(X) is an infinite language}, where <X> represents the encoding of the deterministic finite automata (DFA). Then which of the statement is/are correct?
options: Its complement is recognizable by Turing.
It is context-free but not regular.
questions.solution: Whether a DFA accepts an infinite language is decidable (look for a cycle on a path from start to a final state). A decidable language and its complement are both recognizable. The set of DFA encodings is not shown to be context-free.

questions.title: Incorrect Closure Statements
questions.question: Which of the following statement is/are incorrect?
options: If L is CFL and A is DCFL then L-A is CFL.
The subset of a decidable language is always decidable.
If L and A are DCFL then (complement of L) intersection (complement of A) is CFL.
None of the above are incorrect.
questions.solution: (a) L-A = L ∩ complement(A), and complement(A) is a DCFL but not regular, so CFL ∩ DCFL need not be CFL. (b) A subset of a decidable language can be undecidable. (c) It equals the complement of (L ∪ A); L ∪ A is a CFL and the complement of a CFL need not be CFL. All three are incorrect.

questions.title: Language Reduction
questions.question: Consider some language P in {0,1}* reduces to another language Q in {0,1}*. Which of the following statement is true?
options: A Turing machine that recognizes P can be used to construct a turing machine that recognizes Q.
If Q is decidable then P is decidable.
If P is decidable then Q is decidable.
questions.solution: If P reduces to Q, then a decider for Q gives a decider for P. The converse does not hold.

questions.title: Membership Problems
questions.question:
Consider the following statement:
S1: In phase structured language, membership problem is semi decidable.
S2: In context-free languages, membership problem can be solved in polynomial time.
Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: Type-0 membership is semidecidable (RE). CFL membership is solved by CYK in O(n^3). Both are correct.

questions.title: Reverse and Complement of Languages
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
S1: For a decidable language X, X^R may or may not be decidable.
S2: If X is not recursively enumerable then complement of X must be recursively enumerable.
Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: S1 is false: the reverse of a decidable language is always decidable. S2 is false: both X and its complement can be non-RE.

questions.title: Decidable and Semidecidable TM
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Turing machine.
S1: If there is some Turing machine that accepts every string in L and rejects every string not in L then L is decidable.
S2: If there is some Turing machine that accepts every string in L and either rejects or loops on every string not in L, then L is semi-decidable or computably enumerable (CE).
Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: These are exactly the definitions of decidable (recursive) and semidecidable (RE) languages.

questions.title: Decidable Properties of CFG
questions.question: Which of the following is/are decidable properties of context-free?
options: for context-free grammar X, find if string w is in X.
for context-free grammar X, find if L(X) = phi.
for context-free grammar X, find if L(X) is infinite.
none of the above are decidable properties of context free.
questions.solution: Membership, emptiness and finiteness/infiniteness are all decidable for CFGs.

questions.title: Incorrect Statement on TM Existence
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
S1: There is language for which no TM available. Then surely language will be Not RE.
S2: Language is undecidable if and only there is no HTM (halting TM) available for language.
Which of the following is incorrect?
questions.solution: Both statements are correct (RE iff a TM exists; decidable iff a halting TM exists), so neither is incorrect.

questions.title: Language of Palindrome Grammar
questions.question:
Consider the following grammar:
S -> abSba | bSb | aSa | a | b | epsilon
What is the language generated by above grammar?
questions.answer: The set of all palindromes over {a,b}: L = {w | w = w^R}.
questions.solution: Every production wraps S with matching symbols at both ends (a..a, b..b, ab..ba) or ends with a, b or epsilon in the middle. This generates exactly all even and odd length palindromes.

questions.title: Comparing Three Grammars
questions.question:
Consider the following grammars:
G1: S -> aSc | $B, B -> bBc | $
G2: S -> aaScc | $B, B -> bBc | $
G3: S -> aSc | $B, B -> bbBcc | S
Which of the following is true regarding G1, G2 and G3?
questions.answer: L(G1) = {a^n $ b^m $ c^(n+m)} and L(G2) = {a^(2n) $ b^m $ c^(2n+m)} are non-empty CFLs, while G3 generates the empty language.
questions.solution: In G3, S -> aSc | $B and B -> bbBcc | S never lead to a production with only terminals, so no string is derivable and L(G3) = phi. Options were not provided in the source.

questions.title: Simplifying a CFG
questions.question:
Consider the following context free grammar:
S -> aA | aBB
A -> aaA | epsilon
B -> bB | bbC
C -> B
What will be the equivalent simplified CFG for the given grammar?
questions.answer: S -> aA, A -> aaA | epsilon (equivalently S -> a | aA, A -> aaA | aa after removing epsilon).
questions.solution: B and C never derive a terminal string (B -> bB | bbC, C -> B), so they are useless and S -> aBB is removed. The language is a(aa)*.

questions.title: Property of a Grammar
questions.question:
Consider the following grammar:
S -> AB
A -> BaB | a
B -> bbA
Which of the following is true regarding given grammar?
questions.answer: The grammar is unambiguous (it is LL(1)); all variables are useful and the language is infinite.
questions.solution: A starts with 'a' or 'b' depending on its production, and B always starts with 'b', so each parse decision is determined by one lookahead symbol; hence unambiguous. Options were not provided in the source.

questions.title: Productions in GNF
questions.question:
Consider the following grammar G:
S -> XA | BB
B -> b | SB
X -> b
A -> a
After converting above grammar into GNF how many productions are there in the grammar?
questions.solution: Substitute X: S -> bA | BB. B -> b | bAB | BBB has left recursion; remove it with Z -> BB | BBZ and B -> b | bAB | bZ | bABZ. Then S has 5 productions, A has 1, B has 4 and Z has 8, totalling 18 (the unreachable X -> b is not counted). The count can vary with the conversion method.

questions.title: True Statements on Grammars
questions.question: Which of the following is true
options: A grammar is called ambiguous if (No. of parse trees = No. of left most derivation = Number of Right most derivation) > 1
Production of the form A -> a is known as unit production
CNF is also known as binary standard form
In left-most derivation, right most non-terminal is substituted with its production to derive a string
questions.solution: For a string the number of parse trees equals the number of leftmost and rightmost derivations, and ambiguity means more than one. CNF is also called binary form. A -> a is a terminal production, not a unit production, and leftmost derivation substitutes the leftmost non-terminal.

questions.title: Ambiguity of Two Grammars
questions.question:
Given the following two grammars:
G1: S -> AB | aaB, A -> a | Aa, B -> b
G2: S -> aSbS | bSaS | epsilon
What is true regarding above grammars?
questions.answer: Both grammars are ambiguous. L(G1) = a+b and L(G2) = {w | n_a(w) = n_b(w)}.
questions.solution: In G1, 'aab' has two parse trees (S -> AB with A -> Aa -> aa, and S -> aaB). G2 also gives multiple parse trees for strings like 'abab'.

questions.title: Class of Two Languages
questions.answer: Both L1 and L2 are DCFL (hence CFL) but not regular.
questions.solution: L1 = a^n b^n b^m c^m: match a's with first b's, then remaining b's with c's. L2: push for a's and b's, pop for c's. Both are deterministic.

questions.solution: A PDA accepts by final state, by empty stack, or by a combination of both. 'Transition state' is not an acceptance mode.

questions.title: Equivalence of Automata
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(i) For every NFA N there exists a minimal DFA (M) such that L(N) = L(M)
(ii) For every DFA M there exists a DPDA P such that L(M) = L(P)
(iii) For every DPDA P there exists a NPDA N such that L(P) = L(N)
(iv) For every NPDA 'N' there exists a DPDA 'P' such that L(N) = L(P)
The number of correct statements is
questions.solution: (i), (ii) and (iii) are true. (iv) is false because NPDA are more powerful than DPDA.

questions.title: Equivalent Regular Expression
questions.question: Let r1 = (01*)* be a regular expression. Then which of the following regular expression represents r2 such that L(r1) = L(r2).
questions.solution: (01*)* = epsilon plus all strings starting with 0. (0* + 01*1)* generates blocks of 0 and 01+, which gives exactly epsilon plus the strings starting with 0.

questions.title: Complement of w c w^R
questions.question:
Consider the following language L: L = {w c w^R | w in (a+b)*, c in (a+b)}
The complement of L will be
questions.solution: L is the set of odd-length palindromes with an arbitrary middle symbol, which needs guessing the middle and so is not a DCFL. The complement is accepted by an NPDA (even-length strings, or an odd string with a mismatch) so it is a CFL, and it cannot be a DCFL since DCFLs are closed under complement.

questions.title: Minimum DFA States
questions.question: Consider a language L = {a^(29n+9) | n >= 9} then total number of minimum states in DFA will be
questions.solution: The shortest string has length 29*9+9 = 270, so lengths 0 to 269 each need their own state (270 states). From length 270 onward the pattern repeats every 29 symbols, giving a cycle of 29 states. Total = 270 + 29 = 299.

questions.title: Strings in L*
questions.question: Consider the languages L = {ab, aa, baa} which of the following strings is/are in L*
questions.solution: (a) ab|aa|baa|ab|aa. (b) aa|aa|baa|aa. (d) baa|aa|ab|aa. (c) cannot be split into strings of L (it leaves a lone b at the end).

(i) All finite language are context free language.
(ii) All regular language are finite.
(iii) All DCFL are finite.
(iv) All regular language are DCFL.
(v) There exists some language which are finite and irregular.
The number of correct statements from the above statements are
questions.solution: Only (i) and (iv) are true. Regular languages can be infinite, DCFLs can be infinite, and every finite language is regular.

questions.title: Class of Two Languages
questions.answer: L1 is a DCFL; L2 is a CFL but not a DCFL.
questions.solution: L2 is accepted by an NPDA that guesses which inequality to verify. If L2 were a DCFL, its complement intersected with a*b*c* would give {a^n b^n c^n} as a DCFL, which is false. Options were not provided in the source.

questions.title: Grammars Generating DCFL but not Regular

questions.solution: (a) a^(2n) b^(2n), (b) a^n b^(2n), (c) a^(2n) b^n are DCFL and non-regular. (d) generates (ab)*, which is regular.

questions.title: DCFL Check of Two Languages
options: Both L1, L2 are CFL but not DCFL.
Both L1 and L2 are DCFL but not regular.
questions.solution: L1: track parity of a's; if even, match b's with c's, otherwise accept freely, all deterministic. L2: after the marker c or d the machine knows what to do, so it is deterministic. Both are DCFL and non-regular.

questions.title: Property of Concatenated Palindrome Grammar
questions.question:
Consider the following grammar:
S -> AB
A -> aAa | bAb | epsilon
B -> aBa | bBb | epsilon
Which of the following is correct regarding above grammar?
questions.answer: The grammar generates {w w^R x x^R}, the concatenation of two even-length palindromes. It is a CFL and it is ambiguous.
questions.solution: For 'aaaa' we have A = aa, B = aa; or A = aaaa, B = epsilon; or A = epsilon, B = aaaa, so more than one parse tree exists. Options were not provided in the source.

questions.title: Comparing Three Grammars
questions.question:
Consider the following grammars G1, G2 and G3:
G1: S -> PQ, P -> 0P1 | epsilon, Q -> 1Q2 | epsilon
G2: S -> 0S1 | Q, P -> 1Q2 | epsilon
G3: S -> PQ | Q, P -> 0P1 | 01, Q -> 1Q2 | epsilon
Which of the following is true?
questions.answer: G1 and G3 generate the same language {0^n 1^(n+m) 2^m | n, m >= 0}. G2 generates a different language (Q has no production, so G2 derives nothing).
questions.solution: G1 gives 0^n 1^n 1^m 2^m. G3 gives the same for n >= 1 through S -> PQ, and for n = 0 through S -> Q. In G2, Q has no productions, so no terminal string is derived. Options were not provided in the source.

P = ab + aQ + bR

questions.solution: R = Raba + a gives R = a(aba)*. Q = baQ + bR gives Q = (ba)* b R = (ba)* b a (aba)*. Substituting into P gives the expression above. Options were not provided in the source.

questions.title: Operations on a CFL
questions.question:
Suppose, L is any CFL language on alphabet Sigma = {a,b}, and the following language:
L1 = L - {w x w^R | w, x in {a,b}*}
L2 = L1 . L
L3 = complement(L1) ∪ L
Which of the following is/are correct?
questions.answer: L1 = phi, L2 = phi and L3 = Sigma*, so all three are regular.
questions.solution: Taking w = epsilon, {w x w^R} = Sigma*, so L1 = L - Sigma* = phi. Then L2 = phi . L = phi, and L3 = complement(phi) ∪ L = Sigma*. Options were not provided in the source.

questions.title: Language Accepted by a TM
questions.question:
Let M be a turing machine having Q = {q0, q1, q2, q3, q4} a set of states, input alphabet {0, 1}. The tape alphabets {0, 1, B, x, y}. The symbol B is used to represent the end input string. The initial and final states are q0 and q4 respectively. The transitions are as follows:
1. d(q0, 0) = (q1, x, R)
2. d(q0, y) = (q3, y, R)
3. d(q1, 0) = (q1, 0, R)
4. d(q1, 1) = (q2, y, L)
5. d(q1, y) = (q1, y, R)
6. d(q2, 0) = (q2, 0, L)
7. d(q2, x) = (q0, x, R)
8. d(q2, y) = (q2, y, L)
9. d(q3, y) = (q3, y, R)
10. d(q3, B) = (q4, B, R)
Which of the following statement is true about M?
options: M accepts on L = {0^n 1^m | n, m >= 0}.
M accepts on 011 as a substring.
questions.solution: The machine marks a 0 as x, then marks the matching 1 as y, and repeats. When no 0 is left it checks that only y's remain and moves to the final state. It accepts 0^n 1^n (strictly for n >= 1, as there is no transition on B from q0), so option (c) is the closest.

questions.title: Language of a TM
questions.question:
Consider the following transitions of a turing machine M:
d(q0, a) = (q1, B, R)
d(q0, b) = (q1, B, R)
d(q0, B) = (q3, B, R)
d(q1, b) = (q2, B, R)
d(q1, a) = (q2, B, R)
d(q2, a) = (q0, B, R)
d(q2, b) = (q0, B, R)
The language derived by the equivalent turing machine defined as?
questions.solution: The machine cycles q0 -> q1 -> q2 -> q0 consuming one symbol each time and accepts (q3) only when it sees the blank at q0, so the length must be a multiple of 3.

options: Every NTM (Non-deterministic Turing Machine) can be converted into DTM (Deterministic Turing Machine).
Every DTM (Deterministic Turing Machine) can be converted into NTM (Non-deterministic Turing Machine).
questions.solution: NTM and DTM are equivalent in power; every DTM is trivially an NTM and every NTM can be simulated by a DTM.

questions.title: Halting of Turing Machine
questions.question: Which of the following statement is/are true regarding halting of turing machine?
options: If head of TM always move right, then TM never halts.
If head of TM always move left, then TM may halt.
If head of TM always move left, then TM never halts.
If head of TM moves in right and sometimes in left (loop), then also the TM never halts.
questions.solution: A TM can halt by reaching a final state or a state with no transition regardless of the direction it moves, so only (b) is true.

questions.title: Language of a TM from Transition Table
questions.question:
Given transition table of turing machine is as follow:
-> q0 on 0 -> (q0, 0, R); on 1 -> (q1, 0, R)
q1 on 0 -> (q0, 1, R); on 1 -> (q1, 1, R)
If q0 is initial state and q1 is final state, which of the following language is accepted by given turing machine?
options: Set of all string ending with 1.
Set of all string ending with 11.
Set of all string starting with 0.
Set of all string starting with 10.
questions.solution: The machine moves to q1 exactly when it reads a 1, and returns to q0 when it reads a 0 in q1. So it ends in q1 iff the last symbol read is 1.

questions.title: True Statements on Language Classes
questions.question: Which of the following is/are true?
options: There exist no recursive enumerable language that is recursive language.
If L is CFL, then complement of L may be CFL.
There exist no recursive language that is not recursively enumerable.
If L is CFL, then complement of L may be CSL.
questions.solution: Every recursive language is RE, so (a) is false and (c) is true. The complement of a CFL may be a CFL (e.g. regular languages) and is always a CSL since CSLs are closed under complement.

questions.title: Machines Equal to Turing Machine
questions.question: Which of the following has the same computational power as of turing machine?
questions.solution: A PDA with one additional stack has two stacks in total, which equals a TM. A PDA with 2 additional stacks and an FA with 2 counters are also equivalent to a TM. An FA with one counter is only a restricted PDA.

questions.title: Transition Function of DTM
questions.question:
Which of the following is a correct transition function of DTM?
When Q = Set of state, Sigma = Input alphabet, Gamma = Tape alphabet, F = Final state, delta = Transition function
options: delta: Q x Sigma -> Q x Gamma x F
delta: Q x Sigma -> Q x Sigma x {L, R}
delta: Q x Gamma -> Q x Gamma x {L, R}
delta: Q x Gamma -> Q x Sigma x F
questions.solution: The TM reads a tape symbol, writes a tape symbol, changes state and moves L or R: Q x Gamma -> Q x Gamma x {L, R}.

questions.solution: For r1 the minimum pumping length is 2 (length 1 fails on 'b'). For r2, length 2 fails on 'ab' (pumping up three times leaves a*b*), while length 3 works, so P2 = 3. P1*P2 = 6.

questions.title: Infinite Language Condition
questions.question: Suppose, a language L has finite automata M with N states. The language generated by FA is L(M) is an infinite if and only if we have a string w in L such that
questions.solution: L(M) is infinite iff it contains a string with N <= |w| <= 2N-1 (i.e. N <= |w| < 2N).

questions.title: Regular Grammars
questions.question: Consider the following grammars G1 and G2: G1: S -> aS | S | A, A -> aA | abA | epsilon; G2: S -> aS | a. Which of the following grammar is/are regular?
questions.solution: Both grammars are right linear (every production has the form variable -> terminals followed by at most one variable), so both are regular.

questions.title: Regular Languages
questions.question: Which of the following language is/are regular?
options: L = {a^m b^n | m != n and m != n}
L = {a a^n b^n b b | n >= 1}
questions.solution: LCM(m,n) = 100 has only finitely many solutions, so (c) is finite and regular. The others need unbounded counting.

questions.title: Regularity of Two Languages
questions.question: Consider the following two language L1 and L2. L1 = {www | w in {a}*}, L2 = {{a^(n^n)}* | n >= 1}. Which of the following is correct?
options: Both L1 and L2 are regular.
questions.solution: L1 = (aaa)*, which is regular. L2 includes n = 1, which gives a*, so L2 = a* is regular.

questions.title: Non-regular Language
questions.question: Which of the following language is non-regular?
options: L = {w x w^R | x, w in {a,b}*}
L = {w x w | w, x in {a,b}*}
L = {w x w x | w, x in {a,b}+}
questions.solution: (a) and (b) equal {a,b}* (take w = epsilon). In (c) strings have the form uu with |u| >= 2, which is non-regular.

questions.title: Regular Language from Grammar
questions.question: Consider the following grammar G1 and G2: G1: S -> aAb, A -> aB | epsilon, B -> Ab; G2: S -> aABb, A -> aA | epsilon, B -> bB | epsilon. Which of the following grammar generates a regular language?
questions.solution: G1 generates a^(n+1) b^(n+1), which is non-regular. G2 generates a a* b* b, which is regular.

questions.title: Number of Regular Languages
questions.solution: (1) and (2) have sparse, rapidly growing lengths and are non-regular. In (3), n = 1 gives all lengths m >= 2, and every other length m^n is also at least 2, so L = a^k for k >= 2, which is regular.

questions.title: Language of Grammar G
questions.question: Consider the following grammar G: S -> AB | CD, A -> aaA | epsilon, B -> bB | epsilon, C -> aaC | epsilon, D -> bD | epsilon. The language generated by above grammar is:
questions.solution: The language is (aa)* b*, which is infinite and regular.

questions.title: Non-regular Language
questions.question: Which of the following language is non-regular?
options: L = {a^m b^n X | m, n >= 1, X in {a,b}*}
questions.solution: (a) = (aa)+ (bb)+, (b) = a+ b+ (a+b)*, and (c) includes n = 1 which gives a*, so L = a*. All are regular.

questions.title: Not Regular Language
questions.question: Which of the following language is not regular?
questions.solution: (a) and (b) are {a,b}*, and (c) is the set of even-length strings. All are regular.

L = {w w p | w, p in {0,1}*}

questions.title: Regular Expression of a Language
questions.question: Consider the following given language L. L = {p q w w y r | w, p, q, r in {a,b}*}. The regular expression generated by above language is?
questions.solution: Taking w = epsilon, every string can be written in the form, so L = (a+b)*.

questions.title: Regular Expression of w w p
questions.question: Consider the language L = {w w p | w, p in {a,b}+}. Which of the following regular expression generated by above language?
questions.solution: Strings in L have a prefix that is a square ww followed by a non-empty suffix. Strings such as 'aba' and 'abb' are not of this form, so L is not (a+b)+ or the other listed expressions.

questions.title: Equivalence Classes
questions.question: Consider the following language L: L = {x w | |x| = 2, w in {a,b}*}. For the above language L, how many equivalence classes are possible?
questions.solution: L is the set of strings of length at least 2. Classes: length 0, length 1, length at least 2.

questions.title: Regular Language Among Two
questions.question: Consider the following languages. L1 = {w x w^R | w, x in {a,b}+}, L2 = {w w^R x | w, x in {a,b}+}. Which of the following language is regular?
options: Both L1 and L2 are regular.
questions.solution: L1 is the set of strings of length at least 3 whose first and last symbols are equal, which is regular. L2 needs a prefix w w^R of unbounded length, so it is not regular.

questions.title: Kleene Closure Statements
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
S1: Kleene Closure (*) of infinite set is always finite.
S2: Kleene Closure (*) of finite set is always infinite.
Which of the following is correct?
options: Both S1 and S2 are correct.
questions.solution: The closure of an infinite set is infinite. The closure of a finite set can be finite, e.g. phi* = {epsilon}.

questions.title: Subset of a Language
questions.question: Consider a language L, then subset of L will be?
questions.solution: A subset of a language can be regular or non-regular, so none of the given statements always holds.

questions.title: Union and Intersection of a*b* and b*a*
questions.question: Consider two languages L1 and L2: L1 = a*b*, L2 = b*a*. Which of the following is/are correct for above languages.
options: For L1 ∪ L2 regular expression will be (a+b)*
For L1 ∩ L2 regular expression will be (a* + b*)
questions.solution: Regular languages are closed under union and intersection. The union is not (a+b)* (e.g. 'aba' is missing). The intersection contains only strings of a's alone or b's alone: a* + b*.

questions.title: Language with Regular Subset
questions.question: If subset of L1 is regular then what is L1?
questions.solution: A regular subset tells us nothing about L1; it can be regular or non-regular.

questions.title: Operation Not Closed for Regular Languages
questions.question: Regular language does not close under on which operation?
questions.solution: Regular languages are closed under complement, union and intersection, but not under taking subsets.

questions.title: Complement Statements
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
[I] If L is regular, then complement of L is regular.
[II] If complement of L is regular, then L is regular.
[III] Union of L and its complement is Sigma*.
Number of correct statement is/are
questions.solution: All three statements are true.

questions.title: Operations on {epsilon} and a+
questions.question: Let L1 = {epsilon}, L2 = {a+}. Then which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: L1 ∩ L2 = phi, the union is just a*, and the complement of a+ contains many strings, so (a), (b) and (c) are all false.

questions.title: Language with Regular Kleene Closure
questions.question: Consider a regular language L. If L* = {a}* is regular, then which of the following is true?
questions.solution: The set {a} is finite and hence regular.

questions.title: Closure Properties of Regular Languages
questions.question: Consider a regular language L, which of the following statements are true regarding L.
options: Prefix(L) = {w | w w1 in L, w1 in Sigma*} is regular.
Suffix(L) = {w | w1 w in L, w1 in Sigma*} is regular.
Half(L) = {w | w w1 in L, |w| = |w1|} is regular.
L is closed under infinite intersection.
questions.solution: Regular languages are closed under prefix, suffix and half operations, but not under infinite intersection.

questions.solution: Regular languages are closed under complement, so Sigma* - L1 is regular. The other statements are false.

questions.title: Operations on Languages
questions.question: Let's suppose the languages L1 = {a} & L2 = {phi}. Then L2 L1* ∪ L2*?
questions.solution: Treating L2 as the empty language, L2 L1* = phi and L2* = {epsilon}. The union is {epsilon}.

questions.title: Homomorphism of a Regular Language
questions.question: Consider a regular language L over the alphabet Sigma = {a,b}. L is defined as x = (a+b*)(bab*). If homomorphism h is defined over T = {c,d,e} and h(a) = cd, h(b) = cddec then the regular language h(L) is given as
questions.solution: Replace a by cd and b by cddec: (a + b*) becomes (cd + (cddec)*) and (b a b*) becomes (cddec)(cd)(cddec)*.

questions.title: Union and Infinite Union of Regular Languages
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
S1: if L1 ∪ L2 is regular, then both L1 and L2 are regular.
S2: Regular language is closed under infinite union.
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Both S1 and S2 are false.
questions.solution: S1 is false (a non-regular L1 and its complement-like partner can union to a regular set). S2 is false: regular languages are not closed under infinite union.
